span.label: method
span.quote: Efficient randomized algorithms are given for these two problems on a hypothetical quantum computer.

span.label: prime factorization and discrete logarithms on a quantum computer
span.quote: This paper considers factoring integers and finding discrete logarithms, two problems which are generally thought to be hard on a classical computer and which have been used as the basis of several proposed cryptosystems.

span.label: algorithm-design
span.term: algorithm-design
span.quote: Instead of giving a quantum computer algorithm for factoring n directly, we give a quantum computer algorithm for finding the order of an element x in the multiplicative group (mod n); that is, the least integer r such that xr 1 (mod n).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A THESIS'S VALUE IS ITS ECONOMY, AND THE ECONOMY IS STATED AS THE REASON: Church's thesis GREATLY SIMPLIFIES THE STUDY OF COMPUTATION, SINCE IT REDUCES THE POTENTIAL FIELD OF STUDY FROM AN INFINITE NUMBER OF POTENTIAL COMPUTING DEVICES TO TURING MACHINES. What is claimed for it first is not its truth but what it lets one stop studying
span.quote: Central to this result is Church’s thesis, which says that all computing devices can be simulated by a Turing machine. This thesis greatly simplifies the study of computation, since it reduces the potential field of study from any of an infinite number of potential computing devices to Turing machines.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: FORMALISING A CLAIM WOULD MAKE IT WEAKER, AND THE MECHANISM IS GIVEN: the thesis IS NOT A MATHEMATICAL THEOREM, and to make it one WOULD REQUIRE A PRECISE MATHEMATICAL DESCRIPTION of a computing device - which WOULD LEAVE OPEN THE POSSIBILITY of some practical device NOT SATISFYING that description, and so WOULD MAKE THE RESULTING THEOREM WEAKER THAN THE ORIGINAL THESIS. A formalism can be escaped in a way an informal claim cannot
span.quote: Church’s thesis is not a mathematical theorem; to make it one would require a precise mathematical description of a computing device. Such a description, however, would leave open the possibility of some practical computing device which did not satisfy this precise mathematical description, and thus would make the resulting mathematical theorem weaker than Church’s original thesis.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CATEGORY IS INTRODUCED EXPLICITLY AS A COMPROMISE BETWEEN TWO UNUSABLE GRAINS: the old distinction is MUCH TOO COARSE, the exact efficiency is TOO PRECISE A QUANTITY TO WORK WITH EASILY, and what the field uses is THE GENERALLY ACCEPTED COMPROMISE BETWEEN COARSENESS AND PRECISION - polynomial versus superpolynomial scaling. The class P is presented as a negotiated grain, not a natural joint
span.quote: With the development of practical computers, it has become apparent that the distinction between computable and non-computable functions is much too coarse; computer scientists are now interested in the exact efficiency with which specific functions can be computed. This exact efficiency, on the other hand, is too precise a quantity to work with easily. The generally accepted compromise between coarseness and precision distinguishes efficiently and inefficiently computable functions by whether the length of the computation scales polynomially or superpolynomially with the input size. The class of problems which can be solved by algorithms having a number of steps polynomial in the input size is known as P.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE CLASSIFICATION IS SHOWN TO REQUIRE A FURTHER THESIS BEFORE IT MEANS ANYTHING: FOR THIS CLASSIFICATION TO MAKE SENSE, WE NEED IT TO BE MACHINE-INDEPENDENT - we need to know that polynomial-time computability does not depend on the kind of device used - and that requirement IS a quantitative version of Church's thesis. A definition resting on an unproved claim about the world
span.quote: For this classification to make sense, we need it to be machine-independent. That is, we need to know that whether a function is computable in polynomial time is independent of the kind of computing device used. This corresponds to the following quantitative version of Church’s thesis

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ONE CLAIM CARRIES THREE NAMES ACROSS THREE LITERATURES, AND ONE OF THEM ONLY PARTLY: the same thesis has been CALLED THE STRONG CHURCH'S THESIS by one group, and MAKES UP HALF OF THE INVARIANCE THESIS of another author. Two vocabularies name it whole, a third contains it as a part - which is a partial overlap between naming systems, not a synonym
span.quote: quantitative version of Church’s thesis, which Vergis et al. [1986] have called the “Strong Church’s Thesis” and which makes up half of the “Invariance Thesis” of van Emde Boas [1990].

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A READER-FACING SUBSTITUTION IS OFFERED AND JUSTIFIED BY MUTUAL SIMULATION: readers NOT COMFORTABLE WITH Turing machines MAY THINK INSTEAD OF digital computers with linearly growing memory, BECAUSE THESE TWO CLASSES CAN EFFICIENTLY SIMULATE EACH OTHER. One object is licensed to stand in for another, and the licence is an equivalence
span.quote: Readers who are not comfortable with Turing machines may think instead of digital computers having an amount of memory that grows linearly with the length of the computation, as these two classes of computing machines can efficiently simulate each other.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE THESIS'S ESCAPE CLAUSES ARE LOCATED IN TWO SPECIFIC WORDS AND NAMED AS SUCH: THERE ARE TWO ESCAPE CLAUSES IN THE ABOVE THESIS - ONE OF THESE IS THE WORD PHYSICAL, and machine models that violate the thesis HAVE BEEN RULED OUT BY SOME REASON FOR WHY THEY ARE NOT PHYSICAL, that is, why they could not be built and made to work. **A single underdefined word is doing the excluding**
span.quote: There are two escape clauses in the above thesis. One of these is the word “physical.” Researchers have produced machine models that violate the above quantitative Church’s thesis, but most of these have been ruled out by some reason for why they are not “physical,” that is, why they could not be built and made to work.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AND THE SECOND ESCAPE CLAUSE IS A WORD WHOSE MEANING IS SAID TO BE INCOMPLETELY SPECIFIED: THE OTHER ESCAPE CLAUSE IS THE WORD RESOURCES, THE MEANING OF WHICH IS NOT COMPLETELY SPECIFIED - after which the resources are enumerated for digital computers, and MORE are said to be pertinent to analog computation. The thesis's content varies with a list nobody has closed
span.quote: The other escape clause in the above thesis is the word “resources,” the meaning of which is not completely specified above. There are generally two resources which limit the ability of digital computers to solve large problems: time (computation steps) and space (memory). There are more resources pertinent to analog computation

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A NEW RESOURCE IS ADDED TO THE ACCOUNTING AND THE ADDITION IS ARGUED FOR: for quantum computation, IN ADDITION TO SPACE AND TIME, THERE IS ALSO A THIRD POTENTIALLY IMPORTANT RESOURCE, PRECISION - and the argument is that the changes a quantum computer makes CAN CLEARLY NOT BE PERFECTLY ACCURATE but MUST CONTAIN SOME SMALL AMOUNT OF INHERENT IMPRECISION. The bookkeeping is extended because the physics forces a third column
span.quote: For quantum computation, in addition to space and time, there is also a third potentially important resource, precision. For a quantum computer to work, at least in any currently envisioned implementation, it must be able to make changes in the quantum states of objects (e.g., atoms, photons, or nuclear spins). These changes can clearly not be perfectly accurate, but must contain some small amount of inherent imprecision.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: WHAT SETS THE LIMIT IS ATTRIBUTED TO MATERIALS RATHER THAN TO PHYSICAL LAW, WITH THE HEDGE STATED: AS FAR AS WE KNOW, what precision is possible IS DICTATED NOT BY FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL LAWS BUT BY THE PROPERTIES OF THE MATERIALS AND THE ARCHITECTURE with which the computer is built - and IT IS CURRENTLY NOT CLEAR which architectures will give high precision
span.quote: As far as we know, what precision is possible in quantum state manipulation is dictated not by fundamental physical laws but by the properties of the materials and the architecture with which a quantum computer is built. It is currently not clear which architectures, if any, will give high precision, and what this precision will be.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A MODELLING CHOICE IS DEFENDED AGAINST A TRUE DESCRIPTION, AND THE GROUND IS USEFULNESS: treating precision as a large constant - EVEN THOUGH IT IS ALMOST CERTAIN TO BE CONSTANT FOR ANY GIVEN MACHINE - is compared to treating a digital computer as a finite automaton, of which the verdict is THIS VIEW IS TECHNICALLY CORRECT; HOWEVER, IT IS NOT PARTICULARLY USEFUL. A description can be accurate and the wrong one to adopt
span.quote: Treating the precision as a large constant (even though it is almost certain to be constant for any given machine) would be comparable to treating a classical digital computer as a finite automaton — since any given computer has a fixed amount of memory, this view is technically correct; however, it is not particularly useful.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A KEY WORD IS FOUND SUBSTITUTED IN ANOTHER AUTHOR'S STATEMENT OF THE SAME THESIS, AND THE SUBSTITUTION IS DIAGNOSED: in one restatement THE WORD PHYSICAL IS REPLACED WITH THE WORD REASONABLE - and IT IS DIFFICULT TO IMAGINE ANY DEFINITION OF REASONABLE IN THIS CONTEXT WHICH DOES NOT MEAN PHYSICALLY REALIZABLE. One word swapped for another in the same claim, and the author argues they must come to the same thing
span.quote: This can be seen in the statement of the quantitative Church’s thesis in van Emde Boas [1990], where the word “physical” in the above phrasing is replaced with the word “reasonable.” It is difficult to imagine any definition of “reasonable” in this context which does not mean “physically realizable,” i.e., that this computing machine could actually be built and would work.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A THESIS IS BELIEVED ON THE STRENGTH OF FAILED REFUTATIONS, AND THE FAILURES ARE THEN SHOWN TO SHARE A PROPERTY: computer scientists became convinced THROUGH THE FAILURE OF ALL PROPOSED COUNTER-EXAMPLES - but MOST OF THESE HAVE BEEN BASED ON THE LAWS OF CLASSICAL MECHANICS, HOWEVER THE UNIVERSE IS IN REALITY QUANTUM MECHANICAL. The induction's instances share exactly the property the new case lacks
span.quote: Computer scientists have become convinced of the truth of the quantitative Church’s thesis through the failure of all proposed counter-examples. Most of these proposed counter-examples have been based on the laws of classical mechanics; however, the universe is in reality quantum mechanical.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: PRIORITY IS ASSIGNED BY THE EXPLICITNESS OF A QUESTION RATHER THAN BY THE IDEA, AND ONE AUTHOR IS CREDITED FOR WHAT HE DID NOT ASK: one researcher DID NOT ASK whether quantum mechanics conferred extra power AND YET showed enough to make later work possible; another RAISED THE POSSIBILITY, THUS IMPLICITLY ASKING the converse question; and a third WAS THE FIRST TO ASK THIS QUESTION EXPLICITLY
span.quote: Although he did not ask whether quantum mechanics conferred extra power to computation, he showed that reversible unitary evolution was sufficient to realize the computational power of a Turing machine, thus showing that quantum mechanics is at least as powerful computationally as a classical computer. This work was fundamental in making later investigation of quantum computers possible. Feynman [1982,1986] seems to have been the first to suggest that quantum mechanics might be more powerful computationally than a Turing machine. He gave arguments as to why quantum mechanics might be intrinsically expensive computationally to simulate on a classical computer. He also raised the possibility of using a computer based on quantum mechanical principles to avoid this problem, thus implicitly asking the converse question: by using quantum mechanics in a computer can you compute more efficiently than on a classical computer? Deutsch [1985, 1989] was the first to ask this question explicitly.

span.quote: allowing a small probability of error

span.label: No quantum computer exists that could run the algorithms.
span.quote: Currently, nobody knows how to build a quantum computer, although it seems as though it might be possible within the laws of quantum mechanics.

span.label: Decoherence and precision obstacles grow with machine size, so machines large enough for interesting computations may face fundamental difficulties.
span.quote: Both of these obstacles become more difficult as the size of the computer grows, so it may turn out to be possible to build small quantum computers, while scaling up to machines large enough to do interesting computations may present fundamental difficulties.

span.label: The analysis of the discrete-log algorithm only establishes the residue of r for primes larger than 18, requiring extra work for small prime powers.
span.quote: We will only be able to prove that we can find this remainder for primes larger than 18, but with a little extra work we will still be able to recover r.

span.label: The proved efficiency bounds are loose; an actual implementation could do considerably better than the paper's analysis shows.
span.quote: If one were to actually program this algorithm there are many ways in which the efficiency could be increased over the efficiency shown in this paper.

span.label: The problems solved are of narrow intrinsic value, mattering mainly because cryptography assumed they were hard.
span.quote: Discrete logarithms and factoring are not in themselves widely useful problems.

span.label: Making the thesis provable would make it weaker, and the paper says so: 'Church’s thesis is not a mathematical theorem; to make it one would require a precise mathematical description of a computing device. Such a description, however, would leave open the possibility of some practical computing device which did not satisfy this precise mathematical description, and thus would make the resulting mathematical theorem weaker than Church’s original thesis.' The informal statement is unprovable and the formal one is about a smaller class of machines.

However, if we let the precision grow polynomially in the input size (that is, we let the number of bits of precision grow logarithmically in the input size), we appear to obtain a more powerful type of computer.

span.note: THREE PAPERS, THREE DIFFERENT VERDICTS ON WHETHER A FORMALISM CAN BE SHOWN TO CAPTURE THE INFORMAL NOTION IT REPLACES - and no type in the vocabulary can express a disagreement about what KIND OF CLAIM something is. This paper says the identification CANNOT BE MADE A THEOREM WITHOUT WEAKENING IT: a precise mathematical description of a computing device would leave open the possibility of a practical device that did not satisfy it, so the theorem would be weaker than the thesis it replaced. turing1936-computable-numbers argues it instead, enumerating three kinds of argument; tkacik2016-information-living reports a theorem that did make a vague notion precise. **`same-as` and `distinct-from` are both false here**: the three are not making one claim or two, they are ruling differently on whether the identification is the sort of thing a proof can settle. All eight edge types assert that a relation holds between two concepts. Such a description, however, would leave open the possibility of some practical computing device which did not satisfy this precise mathematical description, and thus would make the resulting mathematical theorem weaker than Church’s original thesis.

span.label: Quantitative Church’s thesis - AS THE PAPER READS IT, WITH ITS TWO LOOSE WORDS NAMED: 'There are TWO ESCAPE CLAUSES in the above thesis. One of these is the word "physical" ... The other escape clause ... is the word "resources," the meaning of which is NOT COMPLETELY SPECIFIED.' What the thesis asserts depends on which senses are supplied for those two words
span.quote: There are two escape clauses in the above thesis. One of these is the word “physical.” Researchers have produced machine models that violate the above quantitative Church’s thesis, but most of these have been ruled out by some reason for why they are not “physical,” that is, why they could not be built and made to work. span.label: contradicts → the quantitative (strong) Church's thesis, that any physical computing device can be simulated by a Turing machine with at most polynomial overhead
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHETHER QUANTUM MECHANICS IS TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT. 'A DIGITAL COMPUTER IS GENERALLY BELIEVED TO BE AN EFFICIENT UNIVERSAL COMPUTING DEVICE; that is, it is believed able to simulate any physical computing device WITH AN INCREASE IN COMPUTATION TIME BY AT MOST A POLYNOMIAL FACTOR. THIS MAY NOT BE TRUE WHEN QUANTUM MECHANICS IS TAKEN INTO CONS[IDERATION].' The thesis is not shown false - it is shown to have a physical precondition nobody had needed to state, and the polynomial factor is what fails. A `contradicts` alone records a dispute with a computing thesis and drops the fact that the dispute is ABOUT WHICH PHYSICS THE MACHINE OBEYS. Q-502.
span.quote: A digital computer is generally believed to be an efficient universal computing device; that is, it is believed able to simulate any physical computing device with an increase in computation time by at most a polynomial factor. This may not be true when quantum mechanics is taken into consideration.
